content.title: Visual guided AI color art image generation using enhanced GAN
content.text:
IntroductionWith the improvement of material living standards, the public demand for color art images continues to grow1. However, traditional manual painting methods are limited by the artist’s inspiration and the time required for creation, which makes it difficult to meet the expanding market demand2. In recent years, the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology to the field of artistic creation has significantly improved the quality and efficiency of image production. As a result, many researchers have applied it to enhance the diversity of artistic creation3. S. Huang et al. designed a new text driven fashion image editing framework called T-FIT to address the issue of false correlations in training data that often lead to changes in other regions when editing regions representing expected editing concepts. T-FIT combines counterfactual reasoning with concept learning to mitigate the impact of false correlations. Numerous experiments have shown that the research method can achieve state-of-the-art performance in various fashion image editing tasks4. C. Jin et al. designed a multi-task artistic benchmark evaluation system based on domain knowledge to reduce the reliance on human prompt engineering in AI art models. This system processes multimodal user queries to improve adaptability to artistic datasets and demonstrates advantages over other models5. L. Yu et al. proposed a framework that integrates a dual-stream content-style processing module, a content-style matching module, and a spatially aware interpolation module based on AI. Their experimental results showed that this model could accurately analyze image styles and generate high-quality stylized images6. Although these methods performed well, they typically require large datasets and computational resources, making them difficult to apply widely in practice. To address this issue, S. Wu et al. put forward a self-driven dual-path framework that used a dynamic pseudo-sample generator to build multi-level correspondences in the color transfer path. Experimental results indicated that the model achieved better style consistency than other advanced methods7. X. Jin et al. proposed a multi focus image fusion framework based on MAMBA to improve fusion quality. The experimental results on synthetic and real datasets show that the research method outperforms state-of-the-art multi focus image fusion methods in terms of quantitative indicators and visual details, verifying that effectively utilizing frequency and depth information can significantly improve the performance of multi focus image fusion8. S. Huang et al. developed a diffusion based causal visual representation learning framework called CIDiffuser to capture causal representations of visual attributes based on structural causal models to address false correlations. The empirical evaluation of two benchmark datasets shows that the research method is significantly superior to state-of-the-art methods, achieving highly controllable image editing by modifying the learned visual representation9. Y. Wang et al. investigated the unique challenges posed by specific cultural heritage scenarios, such as limited labeled data and the need to maintain cultural authenticity, and discussed how style transfer techniques can effectively address these issues. This article also emphasizes the integration of visual style transfer in modern creative contexts, highlighting its potential to revitalize traditional culture through contemporary applications10. Overall, current research on image generation is gradually shifting from holistic generation to semantic guidance, controllable structure, and multi feature fusion. Especially, methods that combine attention mechanisms, causal reasoning, and multimodal alignment provide more efficient and flexible solutions for intelligent generation and editing of visual art images. However, the pseudo sample generator may not fully capture the features of the real image to a certain extent, which may result in errors and affect the quality of the generated image.Although existing methods have made progress in artistic image generation, they still face challenges such as large data requirements, high computational costs, and limited quality of generated images. To overcome these challenges, the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), as an important model in deep learning, shows great potential in visually guided artistic style generation due to its powerful image generation capability11,12. P. Li et al. proposed TellMeTalk, an innovative method for generating expressive speech facial videos based on multimodal input. Numerous experiments have shown that this method can generate high-quality and expressive speech facial videos. Compared with the most advanced methods, the proposed method performs better in terms of video quality and precise synchronization of lip movements13. H. Zhao et al. proposed a new hair editing method called HairManip to address the issue that color and shape differences between source and target hair can sometimes lead to unrealistic results. The experimental results show that, due to the carefully designed network structure and loss function, this method has achieved significant results in editing accuracy and authenticity14. K. Hayawi et al. evaluated and compared two art generation models through a survey targeting end-users. They explored the potential of GANs in generating abstract art and landscape art by using two different GAN architectures. The results show that, in terms of overall quality, the artworks generated by GANs are comparable to those of real artists15. S. Shahriar et al. comprehensively examined recent research findings on using GANs to generate visual art, music, and literary texts, and compared the performance of various GAN architectures. Finally, some key challenges in using GANs for art generation were emphasized, and suggestions were made for future research work16. After combining CNN with GAN, the resulting hybrid model’s strong feature extraction ability helps precisely capture complex image details while improving the stability of the training process. For instance, Z. Y. Wang et al. constructed a CNN–GAN malware detection method to defend against cyberattacks. By visualizing code data, the model significantly improved detection accuracy. Simulation results showed that the model reached a classification accuracy of 97.78%, outperforming comparison models17. J. Zhao et al. applied a CNN–CGAN hybrid algorithm in communication systems. Through end-to-end learning, the model optimized communication processes under unknown channels, successfully reducing bit error rate and packet error rate, and was applied in vehicular network communication18.Based on this, the study puts forward an intelligent model for generating AI art images by combining visual guidance with an improved GAN. The innovation of this study lies in the following aspects: (1) Dynamically adjusting the weights of key regions in the image through an adaptive attention mechanism, enabling the model to more accurately capture local and global features in complex artistic styles19. (2) Combining Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize visual guidance information enhances users’ control over the generation process, thereby generating artistic images that better meet personalized needs. (3) By jointly optimizing multiple loss functions, the visual quality and artistic expression of the generated images have been significantly improved. The study aims to improve the efficiency and artistry of image generation and promote the deep integration of AI and artistic creation. The contribution of the research lies in proposing a modular and interpretable CNN-GAN hybrid architecture, which solves the problems of insufficient feature extraction and unstable training of traditional GANs in artistic image generation. Meanwhile, a dynamic optimization mechanism is designed to quantify and weight key regional features through an adaptive attention mechanism, and to construct a DRL-guided optimizer for interactive control with users. These two components work together to improve generation quality from both the internal feature focus and the external input adjustment levels.Methods and materialsImproved GAN design based on CNNThe GAN is a deep learning framework proposed in 2014 that is widely used for generating high-quality data samples. Since it can analyze low-dimensional data and automatically generate realistic high-dimensional data through layer-by-layer learning, GAN has achieved remarkable results in fields such as color art image generation20. GAN consists of two main components: the generator and the discriminator. These two structures optimize the process through adversarial training. The architecture of the generator is shown in Fig. 1.Fig. 1Operational architecture of the generator and discriminator in GAN.As seen in Fig. 1, the generator in GAN receives a random noise vector and processes it through multiple layers to transform it into high-dimensional data samples. These transformed samples are then input into the discriminator along with real data. The discriminator distinguishes between the two and outputs a probability value to assess the authenticity of the data. In this process, a loss function measures the difference between generated data and real data, enabling adversarial training between the generator and the discriminator. Through continuous optimization, the generator adjusts its parameters to produce fake data that closely resemble real data. The generator maps random noise vectors into images with semantic content through a series of learned convolution transformations, following the general design paradigm of GANs. The noise vector, as an unstructured latent input, provides a high-dimensional and traversable latent space for the generation process. The core function of multi-layer CNNs in generators is to map this unordered latent variable into image data with complex structure and semantics through a series of deconvolution and nonlinear transformations. Therefore, the true object of feature extraction is not the noise itself, but the parameterized mapping relationship from noise to image space learned by the generator CNN during training. As adversarial training progresses, the generator learns how to decode different noise vectors into artistic images with rich visual features that conform to the true data distribution. The loss function of the generator in GAN is expressed in Eq. (1)21.$$LOS{S_G}(D,G)={E_{x\sim {P_{data}}(x)}}[\log D(x)]+{E_{z\sim {P_z}(z)}}[\log (1 - D(G(z)))]$$ (1) In Eq. (1), x represents the input image, \(D(x)\) is the discriminator’s judgment of the input image, z denotes the latent space, \(G(z)\) is the image generated by the generator, \(D(G(z))\) is the probability that the discriminator classifies the generator’s output sample \(G(z)\) as real, \({P_{data}}(x)\) represents the real data distribution, \({P_z}(z)\) denotes the distribution of the latent space, and E represents the expected value. The loss function of the discriminator is given in Eq. (2).$$LOS{S_a}={E_{x\sim {P_{data}}(x)}}[\log (1 - D(G(x)))]+{E_{z\sim {P_z}(z)}}[\log D(G(z))]$$ (2) In Eq. (2), \(D(G(x))\) represents the discriminator’s judgment of the generated image. By analyzing the loss functions of the generator and the discriminator in GAN, the authenticity of generated images is continuously optimized during training. However, GAN struggles to focus on local image features during optimization, which may lead to issues such as over-sharpening of generated images22. Therefore, this study introduces a multi-layer CNN feature extraction network to optimize GAN. The design principle is shown in Fig. 2.Fig. 2Design principle diagram of CNN-GAN structure.As shown in Fig. 2, the generator employs a CNN-based feature extraction network responsible for layer-by-layer upsampling and feature transformation of random noise, in order to capture hierarchical features from low-level edges to high-level semantics, and thus construct high-quality image details. In the discriminator, CNN structure is also used to extract hierarchical features from the input image to accurately distinguish its authenticity. The collaborative process of the entire framework is as follows: the CNN in the generator is responsible for building the image, and its output is sent to the CNN in the discriminator for authenticity analysis; The decision result of the discriminator is fed back to the generator as a loss gradient, which drives its CNN to adjust parameters to generate more realistic images, thereby jointly improving the model’s detail representation and training stability in artistic image generation. Although CNN-GAN captures local features of an image and processes complex images through stacked convolutional structures, it has limitations in capturing global structures. Adaptive Attention dynamically adjusts the focus on different regions of the image, improving its ability to capture the overall structure. Therefore, Adaptive Attention is introduced to optimize CNN-GAN and improve the accuracy of generated images. This mechanism is implemented through a differentiable attention weight matrix, and its specific operation process is as follows: Firstly, the module takes the feature map output by the previous CNN layer as input, and calculates an importance score between 0 and 1 for each spatial position through a 1 × 1 convolution and Sigmoid activation function. The importance is quantified as attention weight, thus dynamically determining the attention area. During the training process, these weights are multiplied element by element with the original feature map to enhance key features and suppress irrelevant backgrounds. The update of the attention weight matrix is not carried out in isolation, but through the joint optimization of backpropagation and the total loss function of the generator, so that the model can automatically adjust its focus based on the differences in style and content between the current generated image and the target, thereby achieving end-to-end key region reinforcement learning without the need for manual annotation. The loss function of Adaptive Attention is given in Eq. (3)23.$${A_{att}}=\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{n} {{{\left\| {a \cdot G({x_i}) - G({x_i})} ight\|}^2}}$$ (3) In Eq. (3), a represents the attention weight matrix, and \({x_i}\) is the feature vector of the input image at the ith spatial position. Optimizing the loss function of Adaptive Attention effectively enhances the quality of generated images24. The mechanism of Adaptive Attention in CNN-GAN image generation is illustrated in Fig. 3.Fig. 3Adaptive Attention optimization process mechanism for CNN-GAN.As seen in Fig. 3, Adaptive Attention first dynamically identifies key regions in an image. The generator automatically detects image information within these regions based on image features. Then, the generator assigns different weight proportions to different image regions and adjusts processing intensity based on the importance and detail requirements of each region. This mechanism enables better focus on key parts of the image, such as textures and edges. Additionally, Adaptive Attention effectively balances image style and content, ensuring that generated images meet high-quality and artistic requirements. To balance the style of generated images, a style loss function is introduced to evaluate the differences in style between the generated and target images. The style loss function is expressed in Eq. (4)25,26.$${L_s}(G)={\sum\limits_{k} {\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{n} {\left\| {{F_k}(G({x_i})) - {F_k}(y)} ight\|} } ^2}$$ (4) In Eq. (4), \({F_k}\) represents the feature representation of the k-th layer, and y denotes the target style image. Additionally, a texture loss function is used to analyze the edge textures of the generated images, as expressed in Eq. (5)27.$${L_t}={\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{n} {\left\| {
abla G({x_i}) - 
abla y} ight\|} ^2}$$ (5) In Eq. (5), \(
abla G({x_i})\) represents the gradient of the generated image, while \(
abla y\) denotes the gradient of the target image. The style and texture loss functions effectively optimize the quality of generated images. To further improve training efficiency and enhance network stability, a batch normalization loss function is introduced. The batch normalization loss function is expressed in Eq. (6).$${L_b}={\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{N} {\left\| { rac{{{b_i} - \mu }}{\sigma } -  rac{{{y_i} - \mu ^{\prime}}}{{\sigma ^{\prime}}}} ight\|} ^2}$$ (6) In Eq. (6), \({b_i}\) represents the input feature map, \(\mu\) is the batch mean, \(\sigma\) is the batch standard deviation, and N is the number of feature maps. The differences between generated and target images are also incorporated into the optimization process through multiple loss functions. The optimization objective function integrates adversarial loss and style loss to further reduce the gap between images, as expressed in Eq. (7)28,29.$${\ell _o}={\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{n} {{w_i} \cdot \left\| {G({x_i}) - {x^ * }_{i}} ight\|} ^2}$$ (7) In Eq. (7), n represents the number of images, \({x^ * }_{i}\) is the target image, \(G({x_i})\) is the generated image, and \({w_i}\) denotes the weight assigned to each image. After optimizing CNN-GAN with multiple functions, an improved CNN-GAN framework is constructed. The architecture of the improved CNN-GAN is shown in Fig. 4.Fig. 4Network structure diagram of improved CNN-GAN.As seen in Fig. 4, the generator in GAN receives random noise as input and processes it layer by layer to increase its dimensionality, eventually generating an image at the output layer. To enhance image details and quality, this study incorporates an Adaptive Attention module and a multi-layer CNN feature extraction network in the generator. The generated image is then input into the discriminator, where it is compared with real images. After multi-level computation, the discriminator outputs a classification result and evaluates image quality based on style and color loss, providing optimization feedback for the generator.Design of visually guided AI color Art image generation modelThe improved CNN-GAN captures both global and local image structures, producing high-quality images. Therefore, it is applied to the automatic generation of AI color art images to ensure unified artistic style. In the improved CNN-GAN, the generator and discriminator achieve collaborative optimization through information exchange during adversarial training, as expressed in Eq. (8).$$I(D,G)={E_{z\sim {P_z}(z)}}[\log D(G(z))] - {E_{x\sim {P_{data}}(x)}}[\log D(x)]$$ (8) Equation (8) represents the information exchange between the generator and the discriminator. To enhance user control over generated images, visual guidance information is incorporated into the input layer of the improved CNN-GAN to improve image generation efficiency. The optimization of the CNN-GAN generator is shown in Fig. 5.Fig. 5The optimization mechanism of CNN-GAN using visual guidance.As seen in Fig. 5, different types of visual guidance enhance the image generation process. First, sketches provide the generator with the overall structure of the image, allowing it to create images that match the target layout. Second, a color palette guides the generator in producing images with a specific color scheme, ensuring consistency with expected colors. Additionally, style images facilitate style transfer, ensuring that generated images align with the target artistic style. Lastly, semantic labels assist the generator in producing images for specific scenes. To ensure that generated images meet color requirements, a hue transformation function is applied, as expressed in Eq. (9).$$H=\arctan \left( { rac{{\sqrt 3 (G - B)}}{{2R - G - B}}} ight)$$ (9) In Eq. (9), H represents hue, R is the red channel, G is the green channel, and B is the blue channel. Saturation and brightness are also evaluated, as shown in Eq. (10).$$\left\{  egin{gathered} S= rac{\Delta }{V} \hfill \ V=\hbox{max} (R,G,B) \hfill \ \end{gathered} ight.$$ (10) In Eq. (10), S represents saturation, \(\Delta\) denotes color difference, and V refers to brightness. After optimizing the colors of the generated image based on the visual guidance, it is also necessary to adjust the color matching degree between the target function and the generated image, as expressed in Eq. (11).$${L_c}={\sum\limits_{{i=1}}^{n} {\left\| {G({x_i}) - {y_i}} ight\|} ^2}$$ (11) Equation (11) represents the color adjustment optimization function between the target image and the generated image. To enhance the impact of user-provided visual guidance on the efficiency of image generation by the CNN-GAN, this study employs DRL to adjust the visual guidance. The underlying principle is illustrated in Fig. 6.Fig. 6Schematic diagram of DRL adjusting visual guidance information.As shown in Fig. 6, DRL learns the optimal policy through interactions between the agent and the environment. By guiding the agent to adjust its behavior policy, DRL aims to maximize the cumulative reward. The agent in DRL interacts with the user to optimize the sketch information. DRL assigns reward signals to semantic labels and utilizes a policy network along with a reward mechanism to optimize the color of the generated image, producing an output that aligns with the desired artistic style. To optimize the generated image, DRL relies on reward signals to guide the optimization process, as expressed in Eq. (12).$$Q({s_t},{a_t}) \leftarrow Q({s_t},{a_t})+\chi ({r_t}+\gamma \mathop {\hbox{max} }\limits_{{a^{\prime}}} Q({s_{t+1}},a^{\prime}) - Q({s_t},{a_t}))$$ (12) In Eq. (12), t denotes the time step, \({s_t}\) is the current state, \({a_t}\) is the action taken under the current state, Q represents the evaluation value of the action under the current policy, \({r_t}\) is the immediate reward obtained after the agent performs the action, \(\gamma\) is the discount factor, \(\chi\) is the learning rate, \(a^{\prime}\) represents all possible actions, and \(\mathop {\hbox{max} }\limits_{{a^{\prime}}} Q\) is the maximum evaluation value among all possible actions. The update process of the policy network in DRL is shown in Eq. (13).$${
abla _	heta }J(	heta )=E\left[ {{
abla _	heta }\log {\pi _	heta }({a_t}\left| {{s_t}} ight.) \cdot {G_t}} ight]$$ (13) In Eq. (13), \(	heta\) represents the parameters of the policy network, \({\pi _	heta }({a_t}\left| {{s_t}} ight.)\) is the probability of the current policy, \({G_t}\) denotes the cumulative reward, and \({
abla _	heta }\log {\pi _	heta }({a_t}\left| {{s_t}} ight.)\) is the gradient of the policy. By applying DRL, the interactive feedback process between the user and the CNN-GAN is significantly enhanced, which greatly improves the model’s operational efficiency. Following this, an automatic AI model based on CNN-GAN is constructed for generating color artistic images. The improved workflow of CNN-GAN for automatic artistic image generation is shown in Fig. 7.Fig. 7AI color art image automatic generation model based on CNN-GAN.As shown in Fig. 7, the generator in the GAN first utilizes the visual information adjusted by DRL to automatically construct the overall structure, color tone, and artistic style of the image. By integrating CNN for multi-level feature extraction, the generator gradually captures both local and global features of the image, thereby identifying fine textures and complex artistic elements. Adaptive Attention dynamically adjusts the focus of the GAN, emphasizing critical details within the image. Based on this rich information, the generator produces an initial artistic image. Then, the discriminator evaluates the generated image by comparing it with the target image, providing feedback for optimization. Through adversarial training with the generator, the discriminator drives continuous refinement of image details and style, ultimately generating images that are both realistic and stylistically consistent. The detailed content of DRL integration is as follows: the state is defined as the difference between the current output image features of the generator and the target visual guidance, such as sketches and palettes; Actions are fine-tuning instructions proposed by the strategic network for guiding information, such as color weights in the palette and the strength of key lines in the sketch; The reward combines image quality assessment indicators such as PSNR and real-time improvement of style loss to drive the continuous optimization of generated images in terms of style consistency and visual fidelity. During the training process, the strategy network interacts with the CNN-GAN environment to apply its output actions to the guidance input of the generator, thereby affecting the next round of image generation. The evaluation of the generated results by the discriminator serves as a key reward signal, which in turn drives the parameter updates of the strategy network, forming a closed-loop, collaborative optimization adaptive control system.Overall, the core of the research method is a CNN-GAN framework integrating multi-layer CNNS, which is optimized through an adaptive attention mechanism and DRL. Structurally, Generator employs a 21-layer CNN-based feature extraction network that takes random noise as input and constructs images with hierarchical features through layer-by-layer upsampling and feature transformation. Inside the generator, an adaptive attention module is integrated. This mechanism is implemented through a differentiable attention weight matrix, which receives the feature map output by the previous CNN layer and uses 1 × 1 convolution and Sigmoid activation function to calculate the importance score between 0 and 1 for each spatial position, thereby quantifying it as the attention weight. These weights are multiplied element by element with the original feature map to dynamically adjust the model’s focus on key regions. Subsequently, the generated image is input into the discriminator. The decision result of the discriminator will be fed back to the generator as a loss gradient, driving its CNN to adjust parameters and conduct joint optimization through multiple loss functions such as style loss and texture loss. In addition, this framework also introduces visual guidance information and uses the DRL module to dynamically adjust this guidance information. DRL defines the difference between the current output feature and the target guidance as the state, defines the fine-tuning instructions for the guidance information as the action, and takes quality indicators such as PSNR and style loss as rewards. The policy network of DRL applies its output actions to the guiding input of the generator, while the evaluation of the discriminator is fed back to the policy network as a key reward signal, thus forming a closed-loop adaptive control system.ResultsPerformance comparison of the CNN-GAN hybrid algorithmTo verify the performance advantages of the improved CNN-GAN hybrid algorithm, this study selected the Paintings Dataset (TPD), a large-scale collection of artworks released by the Visual Geometry Group at the University of Oxford. This dataset contained 80,000 paintings covering various artistic themes and styles, including portraits, landscapes, and still life. Deep Convolutional Generative Adversarial Network (DCGAN), Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Network (SAGAN), and a Generative Adversarial Network combined with U-Net (GAN-UNet) were chosen as baseline algorithms for comparison. The hardware and software used in the experiments were as follows: AMD Ryzen 9 7950X CPU, NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, Ubuntu 20.04 LTS, Python 3.9, TensorFlow 2.1. In addition, the study selected commonly used quantitative evaluation indicators for evaluation, namely PSNR to measure the pixel level quality of generated images, Visual Semantic (VS) similarity to evaluate the semantic consistency between generated images and textual descriptions, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) to detect pixel level errors, F1 value to comprehensively consider accuracy and recall rate, and loss value to monitor the stability of the training process. The CNN network studied in this study consists of 1 input layer, 2 convolutional layers, 2 pooling layers, 2 normalization layers, 3 Relu layers, 2 fully connected layers, 1 softmax layer, and 1 output layer, totaling 14 layers. The discriminator in the GAN network consists of 7 convolutional layers and 1 fully connected layer, while the generator consists of 21 layers, for a total of 29 layers. The study first analyzed the performance of the discriminators in terms of accuracy and precision. The comparison results are shown in Fig. 8.Fig. 8Comparison of accuracy and precision.As shown in Fig. 8(a), in the early stages of training, the discriminator of SAGAN achieved an accuracy of approximately 92% in distinguishing generated images, indicating effective separation between generated and target images. In Fig. 8(b), by the end of training, DCGAN reached a precision of 68.1%, showing that the discriminator still retained a certain ability to distinguish images, but significant differences between generated and target images remained. In Fig. 8(c), GAN-UNet exhibited an accuracy fluctuating between 72% and 74% during iterations 250–450, indicating poor optimization of generated images. In Fig. 8(d), CNN-GAN showed high accuracy in the early stages, but after iteration 205, the accuracy dropped significantly and eventually decreased to 50.4%, with a precision of 49.5%. This result suggested that the differences between generated and target images became minimal, and the discriminator could no longer clearly distinguish between them. Overall, CNN-GAN produced the smallest differences between generated and target images in the later stages, indicating better performance. However, accuracy and precision alone were not sufficient to evaluate image quality. Therefore, Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) was selected as an additional evaluation metric, and the results are shown in Fig. 9.Fig. 9PSNR comparison of four algorithms.As shown in Fig. 9(a), SAGAN reached a small peak PSNR of 25.3 dB at iteration 180. DCGAN fluctuated between 19.6 dB and 21.3 dB during iterations 75–150. CNN-GAN showed a continuous increase in PSNR from 22.5 dB to 34.8 dB, with a total improvement of 12.3 dB, surpassing the comparison algorithms. In Fig. 9(b), all models except DCGAN showed more significant PSNR improvements during the early training stages. CNN-GAN maintained a stable PSNR of 37.4 dB at iteration 100. Overall, CNN-GAN demonstrated superior performance in image quality enhancement. To further evaluate the similarity between generated and target images, the study analyzed style loss and texture loss. The comparison results are shown in Fig. 10.Fig. 10Comparison of style loss and texture loss.As seen in Fig. 10(a), DCGAN had the highest initial style loss, with a value around 1.46. CNN-GAN started with a style loss of 1.11, which decreased steadily and stabilized at 0.19. In Fig. 10(b), DCGAN, GAN-UNet, and SAGAN showed similar texture losses around iteration 100, with values decreasing to 0.38, 0.37, and 0.41, respectively. CNN-GAN started with a texture loss of 0.79, experienced some fluctuations between iterations 110 and 220, and eventually stabilized at 0.18. Overall, CNN-GAN outperformed the other models in both style and texture loss and showed strong stability during training. To more deeply analyze the quality of generated images and assess their perceptual differences from real images, the study used Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) as an evaluation metric. The comparison results are shown in Fig. 11.Fig. 11Comparison of LPIPS results of four algorithms.As shown in Fig. 11(a), DCGAN had an initial LPIPS of 0.74. SAGAN’s LPIPS values crossed those of DCGAN between iterations 220 and 420, with DCGAN showing slightly higher values at the end. CNN-GAN started with an LPIPS of 0.55, slightly lower than GAN-UNet, and steadily decreased to 0.34. In Fig. 11(b), the final LPIPS values of DCGAN, SAGAN, and GAN-UNet were close, with DCGAN being the highest. CNN-GAN stabilized at 0.11 by iteration 900. Overall, CNN-GAN showed better optimization and produced higher-quality images compared to the other algorithms.Performance validation of the AI color Art image generation modelTo evaluate the performance of CNN-GAN in automatic color artwork generation, the study selected Attention Mechanism and Fourier Residual Block based Generative Adversarial Network (AtM-GAN), Vector Quantized Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE), and Cycle-Consistent Generative Adversarial Network (CycleGAN) as comparison models. At the same time, a self built dataset of 5,625 color art images was developed, covering six styles including portrait, landscape, abstract art, and still life. The images were sourced from numerous publicly available datasets, with each image having a resolution of 1024 × 1024. The dataset was divided into training (3,938 images), validation (844 images), and test (843 images) sets. In addition, the images were sourced from public art resource platforms such as WikiArt, Google Art Project, The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Met) Open Access, and Smarthistory. In the preprocessing stage, the study performed data augmentation operations such as format unification, bilateral filtering denoising, histogram equalization color enhancement, center cropping, and random rotation on all images. The experiments were conducted using Windows 10, an Intel Core i9-13900 K CPU, and an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, with Python 3.9, PyTorch 1.2, and CUDA 11.2 (NVIDIA CUDA Toolkit 11.2, https://developer.nvidia.com/cuda-11.2.0-download-archive) as the software environment. To evaluate model performance, Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) was used. The results are shown in Fig. 12.Fig. 12SSIM comparison of four models.As shown in Fig. 12(a), the SSIM values of the VQ-VAE model fluctuated between 0.25 and 0.46 at generation 10, then stabilized at generations 50 and 100. In Fig. 12(b), the AtM-GAN model showed greater fluctuations at generation 50, with SSIM values ranging from 0.48 to 0.69. In Fig. 12(c), CycleGAN achieved a maximum SSIM of 0.58 and a minimum of 0.43 at generation 10. In Fig. 12(d), CNN-GAN showed the least fluctuation, with an average SSIM of 0.52 at generation 10, 0.66 at generation 50, and 0.85 at generation 100. Overall, CNN-GAN outperformed the other models in performance and exhibited better stability and convergence during training. To further validate the quality of generated images, the study used Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) as an evaluation metric. The results are presented in Fig. 13.Fig. 13FID comparison of four models.In Fig. 13(a), the VQ-VAE model showed the most significant FID drop during iterations 280–450, decreasing from 53.4 to 40.6. CNN-GAN started with an FID of 62.7, lower than the other models. During iterations 100–155, the FID decreased slowly but dropped more significantly between iterations 250–450, from 47.4 to 35.9. In Fig. 13(b), CycleGAN had the highest FID peak in the early stages at 56.5 and decreased to 28.2 by the end. CNN-GAN showed a sharp drop in FID between iterations 250 and 450 and finally stabilized at 19.5. Overall, CNN-GAN generated higher-quality images than the other models. To measure the diversity of generated images, the study used Inception Score (IS) as an evaluation metric. The results are shown in Fig. 14.Fig. 14IS comparison of four models.As shown in Fig. 14(a), the IS values of VQ-VAE fluctuated between 1.11 and 1.24 at generation 20. CNN-GAN achieved the highest IS values among all models, with an average of 3.52 at generation 20, 5.54 at generation 120, and 7.41 at generation 220. In Fig. 14(b), the IS values of VQ-VAE at generations 20 and 120 were more scattered than at generation 220. CNN-GAN had an IS of 4.02 at generation 20, 6.62 at generation 120, and 8.08 at generation 220, which was 0.67 points higher than the IS value observed in the training set. Overall, CNN-GAN consistently demonstrated significant performance advantages during training, further proving its effectiveness in image generation tasks. This visual contrast strongly confirms the conclusion of the quantitative analysis mentioned above, indicating that this model has significant advantages in capturing complex artistic styles.DiscussionTo optimize the generation patterns of AI-generated color artistic images, this study put forward a novel automatic artistic image generation model by combining CNN with GAN. The model fully utilized the advantages of CNN in image processing and feature extraction, and enhanced GAN’s ability to recognize image detail features. This effectively avoided the instability and image distortion problems that commonly occurred during the training process of traditional GAN models. Experimental results showed that the GAN-CNN model significantly outperformed the traditional GAN model in both convergence efficiency and the quality of automatically generated color artistic images. In the validation using the publicly available art dataset from the University of Oxford, the recognition accuracy and precision of the GAN-CNN model decreased most rapidly, by 36.3% and 30.6% respectively. This indicated that the difference between the generated and real images was minimal, and the optimization efficiency was the highest. In comparison, D. Song et al. in 2023 raised a dual-branch GAN model based on multi-scale connection, which optimized GAN by analyzing spectral spatial features30. However, the proposed GAN-CNN model showed better stability during training and inference. At the end of training, the PSNR of the GAN-CNN model remained stable at 37.4dB, and the texture loss decreased from 0.79 to 0.18, demonstrating a significant improvement in image quality. Compared with the adversarially robust GAN model proposed by S. H. Choi’s team in 2022, which improved defense capability by optimizing generator parameters and obtaining a joint loss function31, this study focused on optimizing style loss and texture loss of artistic images to enhance the quality of image generation. In the LPIPS comparison, the LPIPS value of the GAN-CNN model decreased to 0.34 at the 900th iteration. Meanwhile, on the self-constructed dataset containing 5,625 color artistic images, the GAN-CNN model achieved an SSIM of 0.85 at generation 100, which outperformed the comparison models. The FID value stabilized at 19.5, and the IS score increased from 4.02 at generation 20 to 8.08 at generation 220. In the comprehensive evaluation indicators, the PSNR reached 41dB, VS was 0.79, and the loss value was 0.52, all of which were clearly better than those of the comparison models.The innovation of this study lies in the hybrid model combining CNN and GAN, which fully utilized CNN’s advantages in image processing and feature extraction while optimizing the structure of traditional GAN. First, DRL was introduced to dynamically adjust visual guidance, automatically shaping the overall structure, tone, and artistic style of the image, which made the generation process more intelligent. Second, the multi-layer feature extraction ability of CNN effectively enhanced the generator’s performance in both local and global feature extraction, thereby improving the quality of image details. At the same time, Adaptive Attention dynamically adjusted the focus area, enabling the model to flexibly analyze and optimize image details, thereby improving the accuracy of the generated outputs. Finally, through adversarial training between the generator and the discriminator, the GAN-CNN model continuously improved the generator’s performance in optimizing image details and style, thus achieving high-quality image generation with style consistency. Specifically, the PSNR remained stable at 37.4dB during training, and texture loss decreased from 0.79 to 0.18, proving the stability and efficiency of the proposed method in visual quality and image generation. Therefore, the GAN-CNN-based automatic color artistic image generation model not only better analyzed and reproduced diverse artistic styles but also showed significant innovation in optimizing image quality, improving training stability, and maintaining style consistency.Limitations and future workHowever, research still has certain limitations, as current models may encounter issues such as insufficiently realistic details or lack of style consistency when generating artistic images with highly complex textures and intricate structures. In addition, the model still relies heavily on large-scale datasets during the training process, which to some extent limits its application in resource constrained environments. In future research, optimization can be achieved by introducing a multi-scale convolution module based on U-Net to enhance the control over image details, thereby better generating complex textures and fine details. Secondly, explore more efficient data augmentation techniques to reduce reliance on large-scale datasets. Finally, combining lightweight technology to optimize the model structure, reduce computational costs, and make it more suitable for deployment in resource limited environments. These improvements are expected to further enhance the model’s applicability and practicality in artistic image generation, offering stronger technical support for diverse artistic creation.ConclusionTraditional color artistic image creation is often constrained by the artist’s inspiration and time limitations, making it difficult to meet the growing demand in the market. Therefore, this study introduced a CNN multi-layer network module to optimize GAN, adjusted visual guidance information through DRL, and dynamically adjusted the focus area of GAN using Adaptive Attention. This approach accurately captured key image details and ensured consistency in artistic style. Experimental results showed that the GAN-CNN model significantly outperformed the comparison models in key indicators such as PSNR, FID, Loss, RMSE, and SSIM. Specifically, the RMSE was optimized to 3.9, and the Loss remained stable at 0.52. Additionally, the GAN-CNN model was capable of generating images with unified style and rich artistic features, with a noticeable reduction in deviation from the target images compared to other models. This provides an innovative approach to the field of AI and artistic image generation and opens up new paths for the diversity of artistic image development. However, the model still has limitations when dealing with tasks that require high precision and intricate details in artistic images. In the future, U-Net-based multi-scale convolutional blocks will be introduced to enhance the control of image details and further optimize the generation of complex textures and intricate details in artistic images, aiming to achieve multi-level artistic expression in generated images.
